title: Ship it! Building Production Ready Agents — Mike Chambers, AWS

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core focus is agent anatomy—model, prompt, loop, history, tools—and mapping those components to a managed agent harness via Amazon Bedrock Agents. The content centers on AWS Bedrock and Lambda as developer platform infrastructure for building and deploying production agents. The talk progresses from a local single-file Python prototype to cloud-scale production deployment on managed Bedrock infrastructure. Requires Python and basic LLM knowledge but explains agent fundamentals from first principles with live demos. Recorded conference presentation with live coding demos at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Ten evidence anchors with direct transcript excerpts and character positions support the classification.

summary: Mike Chambers, AWS developer advocate focused exclusively on generative AI, delivers a practical talk on deploying AI agents to production at cloud scale. He opens with a live demo of a minimal agent: a single Python file with a dice-rolling tool running locally on his laptop using the Llama 3.1 8B parameter model. The agent accepts natural language input (e.g., "roll for initiative and add a dexterity modifier of five"), interprets intent using the LLM, invokes the dice-rolling tool, and returns a computed result (d20 roll of 10 plus 5 equals 15). Chambers dissects the anatomy of an agent into five minimal components: the model, the prompt, the agentic loop (a while loop with string manipulation), conversational history (critical for the agent's own reasoning context across steps, not just session memory), and tools. He transitions to Amazon Bedrock, which provides access to models from Anthropic, Amazon Nova, Meta, Mistral, and AI21 Labs. Bedrock Agents is a fully managed service handling the model, prompt, loop, and history automatically. Tools are implemented as action groups backed by AWS Lambda functions. Chambers then performs a real-time console walkthrough: creating an agent named for tabletop RPG assistance, selecting Anthropic Haiku 3.5 as the model, entering instructions ("you're a games master who can help me play tabletop RPG games"), creating an action group with a roll-dice tool requiring an integer parameter for number of sides, and writing Python code in the Lambda function. He notes that action group and parameter descriptions are written in natural language because the LLM reads them to decide tool usage. Amazon Q Developer is built into the console code editor and assists with code suggestions and completion. He deploys the Lambda function, prepares the agent (noting alias IDs and SDLC support for production), and tests it live, getting the expected result of 15. He emphasizes this agent is now fully hosted in a managed environment at cloud scale. He closes by mentioning free DeepLearning.AI courses with a free AWS environment for hands-on Bedrock practice, and invites further discussion about MCP servers at cloud scale and a new open-source SDK for model-first agents.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: A minimal viable agent requires five components: model, prompt, agentic loop, conversational history, and tools.
Conversational history is critical not just for cross-session memory but for the agent's own step-by-step reasoning context within a single interaction.
Amazon Bedrock Agents is a fully managed service that handles model hosting, prompt templating, the agentic loop, and history automatically with no infrastructure to manage.
Action groups in Bedrock are collections of tools backed by AWS Lambda, which scales automatically and can interact with any AWS service or external system.
Tool and parameter descriptions in Bedrock are written in natural language because the LLM reads them to determine when and how to use each tool—a new programming paradigm of definitions and schemas.
Amazon Q Developer is built into the AWS console code editor and can generate code suggestions and completions for Lambda functions.
Bedrock Agents supports alias IDs and a software development lifecycle, enabling different versions for staging and production.
ClickOps via the AWS console is useful for demonstration but production deployments should use Infrastructure-as-Code tools like Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, SAM, or SDKs.
Free DeepLearning.AI courses provide a free AWS environment for hands-on practice with Amazon Bedrock agents.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Mike Chambers introduces himself as an AWS developer advocate specializing in generative AI. He mentions co-creating a fundamentals of LLMs course with Dr. Andrew Ng taken by over 370,000 people. He sets up the talk's theme: showing developers how to get agent code to cloud scale, and showing leaders how to get their developers there.

sections.title: Local Agent Demo
sections.summary: Chambers demonstrates a simple agent in a single Python file with a dice-rolling tool. The agent uses Llama 3.1 8B running locally on his laptop. He shows the system prompt with tool descriptions and few-shot examples (needed because the tiny model needs help understanding tool use). Running the agent, he inputs a tabletop RPG command ('roll for initiative and add a dexterity modifier of five'), and the agent interprets the request, calls the dice tool, rolls a d20 (getting 10), adds 5, and returns 15.

sections.title: Anatomy of an Agent
sections.summary: Chambers breaks down the minimal components of an agent: (1) Model for natural language understanding, (2) Prompt to explain purpose and personality, (3) Agentic loop—the ability to think, use tools, evaluate results, and iterate (essentially a while loop with strings), (4) History—conversational history critical not just for cross-session memory but for the agent's own reasoning steps within an interaction, and (5) Tools for agency to interact with the outside world. He argues these are the base fundamentals for a minimal viable agent.

sections.title: AWS Bedrock for Cloud-Scale Agents
sections.summary: Chambers explains how AWS services map to agent components. Amazon Bedrock provides access to models from Anthropic, Amazon Nova, Meta, Mistral, and AI21 Labs. Amazon Bedrock Agents is fully managed with no infrastructure to manage—it handles the model, prompt (via 'instructions' combined with a default or editable prompt template), loop, and history automatically. Tools are configured as action groups (collections of tools) backed by AWS Lambda, which scales automatically and can interact with any AWS service or external system.

sections.title: Console Demo and Production Considerations
sections.summary: Chambers begins a real-time walkthrough of building the agent in the AWS console, acknowledging that ClickOps is not appropriate for production and noting that everything shown can also be done with Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, SAM, or SDKs for Infrastructure-as-Code.

sections.title: Console Demo: Creating and Configuring the Agent
sections.summary: Chambers walks through creating a Bedrock agent in the AWS console in real time. He names it and gives it a description (an agent to help play tabletop RPG). He selects Anthropic Haiku 3.5 as the model—small, capable, fast, probably more than needed for this demo. He enters instructions ('you're a games master who can help me play tabletop RPG games'), which get combined with the template to form the actual prompt. He then creates an action group, emphasizing that names and descriptions are read by the LLM in natural language to determine tool usage—a new paradigm of programming with definitions and schemas.

sections.title: Console Demo: Defining Tools and Lambda Code
sections.summary: Chambers defines the roll-dice tool within the action group, adding an integer parameter for number of sides marked as required. He uses the Lambda quick start option which automatically sets up the Lambda function, permissions, and agent integration. He writes Python code in the console editor, noting that Amazon Q Developer is built in and provides code suggestions and completions. The code imports random, reads the event to determine which function is called, grabs the number of sides parameter, generates a random number, and formats the response body. He clicks deploy to save the Lambda function.

sections.title: Console Demo: Preparing, Testing, and Closing
sections.summary: Chambers prepares the agent, noting that Bedrock supports alias IDs and a full software development lifecycle for publishing agents. He tests the agent live with flowery language, and it returns the expected result of 15—now running in a fully managed, cloud-scale environment. He closes by mentioning free DeepLearning.AI courses with a free AWS environment for hands-on Bedrock practice, invites discussion about MCP servers at cloud scale and a new open-source SDK for model-first agents, and offers a real D20 at the AWS booth.
